turns.text: The previous story examined Mask R-CNN. Now the camera turns to FPN and RetinaNet and a new question along the same timeline: Turn the clock back to 2017. What problem was FPN and RetinaNet actually trying to solve?

Detectors needed features at multiple scales, but image pyramids were expensive and deep feature maps lost fine spatial detail. Dense one-stage detectors also suffered from extreme imbalance between easy background examples and rare foreground objects.
That sounds like a promising direction. What mechanism actually makes it work?

FPN combines a top-down pathway with lateral connections to build semantically strong maps at several resolutions. RetinaNet pairs that pyramid with focal loss, reducing the influence of easy negatives so hard detection examples drive learning.
Why did the idea outlive one paper or experiment? What did later researchers actually inherit?

Experts generally treat FPN as a standard multiscale backbone and focal loss as a decisive fix for one-stage detector imbalance. Together they narrowed the accuracy gap between one-stage and two-stage detection.
FPN and RetinaNet mattered not only as a result, but as a method that later researchers could test, adapt, and extend.
